text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency Nawaf Salam, president of the
Council of Ministers of the Lebanese
Republic.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
>> Mr. Mr. President, Mr. Secretary
General, the more I reflect on the theme
of this session of the General Assembly,
restoring trust and managing
transformation, a United Nations that
delivers for all,
the more convinced I become of the
wisdom of that choice.
Without mutual trust, peace and security
cannot take root among states,
nor can cooperation among them flourish.
More than 80 years ago, the United
Nations was founded on the promise that
the force of law would replace the law
of force. Yet, we still live in a world
of multiplying wars and conflicts.
A world that spends more on armaments
than on development.
Civilians remain the primary victims
while millions face displacement,
hunger, and deprivation.
The problem is not the absence of rules.
It is their selective application if not
their outright non-application.
The sovereignty of states cannot be
untouchable in one place and negotiable
in another. Nor can the rules of
international law apply to some but not
to others.
Restoring trust requires respect for
international law. It requires
investment in preventing conflicts
before they erupt and in development
before poverty and deprivation become a
source of violence, extremism and
terrorism.
Development too is a matter of peace.
There can be no sustainable peace in a
world of widening economic disparities
where some states spend more on
servicing their debt than on the health
of their citizens and education of their
children.
This does not absolve developing
countries of the responsibility to
undertake reform, combat corruption and
build institutions. But those efforts
require a fairer and more equitable
international economic order, one that
offers them genuine opportunities to
advance. Mr. President, our shared
responsibility is equally evident in the
face of the profound transformations our
world is undergoing.
Climate change threatens the lives and
livelihoods of millions.
Those
countries that have contributed least to
it bear its gravest consequences. This
calls for equitable adaptation, finance,
and technology transfer. At the same
time, the artificial intelligence
revolution is opening unprecedented
horizons for progress across every
sphere of life. Yet it also raises
challenges for the future of work and
for human rights and fundamental
freedoms. This calls for international
governance that places the human being
with his or her freedom and privacy at
the heart of this transformation. Above
all, we must not allow an artificial
intelligence divide to emerge on top of
the existing gaps in wealth and
development. Restoring
trust requires that every individual
feel that the law protects them, that
development do not exclude them, and
that progress leaves no one behind.
Mr. President, if restoring trust is a
challenge facing our world today, for
Lebanon, it is not a mere slogan.
Just as managing transformation is not
an option up for debate together. They
constitute the very essence of the
mission we pledged before our people
before our Arab brothers and before the
entire world on the day I was entrusted
with leading the government of Lebanon.
We assumed it this responsibility at a
time when our country faced three
existential challenges.
The first was to regain the trust of its
people after the financial collapse and
the Beirut port explosion and the
tragedies and wounds they left behind.
The second was to reclaim its national
decision-m so that no authority stands
above that of the state. No weapons
exist outside its armed forces and no
decision on war and peace is taken
outside its constitutional institutions.
The third was to recover all of its
territory from Israeli occupation and to
extend its sovereignty over the entirety
of its national soil through its own
forces in implementation of the ty
agreement and insincere respect for the
relevant international resolutions on
Lebanon. Foremost among these is
resolution 1701 which remains to this
day a fundamental point of reference
governing relations between Lebanon and
Israel.
Trust rebuilt, decision-making
reclaimed, land liberated. That is the
equation for Lebanon's recovery.
These are not three separate challenges.
They are three facets of a single cause.
Restoring a state that its citizens
trust, that is master of its own
decisions, and that exercises
sovereignty over the whole of its
territory.
Mr. President,
first the trust we seek to restore is
not trust in words. It is trust in
institutions that protect rights in a
judiciary that guarantees justice in an
economy that restores prosperity to the
people and gives young people the
opportunity of a better future. We
cannot speak um of restoring trust
without recalling the Beirut port
explosion. The wound of the 4th of
August remains open. It cannot heal
without truth, justice and
accountability and these will inevitably
come.
Some might feel may feel that our
government has not yet fulfilled all of
its commitments. We do not claim that
the task is complete, but fairness
demands that we not overlook the scale
of legacy we inherited, paralyzed
institutions,
a public administration of diminished
effectiveness, an economy stripped of
the foundations of growth, and a state
weakened by compounding crisis and by
decades of external interference.
Even though we have not used the
difficulty of our circumstances as a
pretext to retreat from our commitments
and we will not retreat. Lebanon has
launched reforms on several fronts,
namely revitalizing the public
administration, strengthening the
independence of the judiciary,
modernizing the media law, and
abolishing the death penalty. It is also
advancing towards the completion of
financial reforms aimed at restoring
order to the financial system and
recovering depositors funds. These
reforms should pave the way for an
agreement with the IMF. Such an
agreement is an indispensable tool for
restoring international confidence in
Lebanon and a gateway to securing the
financing needed from all our regional
and international partners for economic
recovery and reconstruction.
Our aim in pursuing reform is not to ask
our people to renew their trust in the
state. Rather, through reform, we seek
to rebuild
a state worthy of its people's trust.
Second,
a state does not regain the trust of its
citizens through reform alone,
but also by reclaiming its national
decision making.
In that spirit, we did not merely affirm
the principle that weapons must be
exclusively in the hands of the state
and that decisions on war and peace rest
solely with its constitutional
institutions. We translated that
commitment into decisions taken by the
council of ministers notably in August
and September of last year and again in
March of this year. That was after
Lebanon found itself in a war that it
did not choose. It was imposed upon us
despite our repeated warnings
again. Repeated warnings of the dangers
of being drawn into it.
As the war in the region widened
and initiatives to end it multiplied, we
held fast to a non-negotiable principle.
No one speaks for Lebanon
and no one negotiates on its behalf
except the Lebanese state through its
constitutional institutions.
It is true that Lebanon is affected by
developments in its surroundings.
>> It is true that Lebanon is affected by
developments in its surroundings.
That does not mean, however, that we
accept it's becoming once again an arena
for the conflicts of others or a burning
chip bargaining chip in their hands.
Lebanon's future
will not be decided on its behalf, nor
may its security and stability become
the price of settlements concluded in
its absence. Third, our position on the
war has been clear from the outset. We
want it to end. We want the ceasefire
consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw
from all Lebanese territory up to our
internationally recognized borders in
accordance with the 199 with the 1949
general armistice agreement and as
firmed by resolution 1701. We want the
release of all our detinees,
the safe and dignified return of our
people to their villages and towns and
the reconstruction of what the war has
destroyed.
It was in that spirit that the Lebanese
state entered into negotiations with
Israel under the kind opices of the
United States of America and its
president for which we are grateful with
a view to reaching arrangements that
ensure an end to the war and the
restoration of Lebanon's full
sovereignty. The sovereignty to which we
are committed is indivisible. It
requires Israel's withdrawal from all
Lebanese territory. It equally requires
the extension of the authority of the
Lebanese state through its own forces
over the entirety of its territory with
weapons held by the state alone. It is
on these two principles and on the basis
of reciprocity and phased implementation
that the tripartite framework reached in
the negotiations rest.
However, the success of any agreement is
measured not by declared intentions but
by fulfillment of commitments.
What is required today therefore is to
complete the translation of this
framework into practical steps within a
clear timetable
and with a verification mechanism that
ensures the implementation of all its
provisions.
Mr. Mr. President, in this context, I
must pay tribute to the role played by
the United Nations interim force in
Lebanon, UNIFIL, and to the courage of
its leadership, personnel, and staff,
and their sacrifices in preserving
stability, supporting the Lebanese armed
forces, and implementing resolution
To all the countries that have
contributed troops to this force,
Lebanon extends its profound thanks and
appreciation.
We have taken note of security council
resolution 2790
of 2025 which decided to terminate
UNIFIL's operations at the end of this
year and to begin its gradual withdrawal
and requested the secretary general to
explore available options for the
continued implementation of resolution
What we wish to stress here and today is
the need to avert the vacuum that
UNIFIL's withdrawal could create
were it to take place without agreement
on a new international force to replace
it.
Such a force should ensure the
continuation of monitoring, reporting
and leaison functions and its role
should complement the requirements for
implementing the tripartite framework.
Mr. President, recovering the Mr.
President, recovering the land does not
mean only the withdrawal of occupying
forces. It also means the return of its
inhabitants and the revival of life in
their villages and towns. The war has
left behind a vast humanitarian crisis
in Lebanon. It has caused extensive
destruction to housing, public
facilities, infrastructure, and
productive sectors, and has deprived
large numbers of Lebanese of their homes
and livelihoods.
While we thank the United Nations
entities and our international partners
for for their humanitarian
contributions, we call at the same time
for continued funding to meet the basic
needs of those affected,
particularly the displaced in parallel
with the requirements of early recovery
as well as reconstruction and
development.
The reconstruction of the south is not
merely the rebuilding of stone. It is
the rebuilding of people's lives, the
restoration of their livelihoods, and
the affirmation of the right to live in
safety and dignity on their land.
Mr. President,
the Lebanon that stands before you today
does not shook its responsibilities, nor
does it ask others to do what
it is duty bound to do itself. We are
shouldering our responsibility for
reform and for extending the authority
of the state over the entirety of our
territory. But we are entitled to ask
the international community to shoulder
in turn its responsibility to ensure
respect for Lebanon sovereignty and the
implementation of resolutions of
international legitimacy.
Mr. President,
there can be no lasting stability in
Lebanon without lasting stability in our
region.
And there can be no stability in the
region as long as this organization
remains unable to enable the Palestinian
people to exercise their inalienable
right to self-determination.
Like all other peoples of the world,
no less and no more.
This is despite the dozens of
resolutions adopted by this assembly and
by the security council that lay clear
foundations for that right, not to
mention the Arab peace initiative.
As for the tragedy of wounded Gaza, it
has put the conscience of the world and
the import uh inability of its
institutions to a test from which there
can be no escape.
I must stress here that cutting off
funding to UNRA or undermining its
mandate does not uh end the rights of
Palestinian refugees,
even if that's what some seek. On the
contrary, it compounds their suffering,
jeopardizes the prospects for a just and
lasting solution to their cause, and
increases the burden on host countries,
foremost among them Lebanon. With regard
to the security situation or region,
Lebanon wishes to renew its solidarity
with the states of the Arab Gulf and
with Jordan in the face of Iranian
attacks that threaten regional security
and the freedom and safety of maritime
navigation.
The effects of these attacks are not
confined to
theaters of confrontation. They extend
to supply chain, to the prices of goods,
particularly food and energy, and to
inflation rates.
Mr. President, allow me to conclude by
returning once more to the theme of this
session of the General Assembly,
restoring trust and managing
transformation
for United Nations that delivers for
all.
The truth
is that we cannot call on the states of
the world to change their conduct while
failing to make the necessary changes
within our own organization so that it
delivers the results expected of it and
regains the trust of the peoples of the
world.
The reality
is that the world has changed profoundly
since 1945.
The membership of the United Nations has
grown nearly four-fold.
Colonialism has ended. Africa has risen.
Asia has been transformed and new powers
have emerged. The balance of the global
economy has shifted. Yet the basic
composition of the security council
remains captive to a historical moment
dating back to the end of the Second
World War.
Africa and the Arab world cannot remain
without permanent representation on the
council, nor can small and medium-sized
states remain mere spectators to
decisions that concern their security
and the f and their future. We know that
security council reform is a complex
matter. But the difficulty of reform
is no argument against its necessity.
Indeed, reform of the United Nations
must begin here with the security
council
for it is the security council that
bears primary responsibility for the
maintenance of international peace and
security. are therefore once again add
Lebanon's voice to that of the majority
of the members of our of our
organization in calling for an expansion
of the security council that achieves
more inclusive and equitable
representation.
Being realists, we do not call for the
abolition of the V2.
Rather, we call for restraint in its use
in cases of genocide, war crimes, crimes
against humanity, and serious violations
of international humanitarian law.
We insist on reform of the United
Nations only because
we
want it to be a more representative,
more democratic, and more effective
organization.
We want an organization true to the
purposes and principles of its charter
yet ever renewed so that it may rise to
the challenges of our rapidly changing
world and meet the aspirations of our
peoples and their new generations. I
thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president of the Council of
Ministers of the Lebanese Republic.
